CHAPTER I Foundations of the Art The elementary vocabulary upon which all else in this book is built. Know these first, for every later term presumes them. No. 1 Artificial Intelligence (AI) The broad discipline of building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human judgment — perceiving, reasoning, deciding, and generating language. No. 2 Machine Learning (ML) A branch of AI wherein a program improves its performance on a task by learning patterns from data, rather than following rules written explicitly by hand. No. 3 Deep Learning A subfield of ML using neural networks of many stacked layers to learn increasingly abstract representations of raw data, such as pixels or words. No. 4 Model The artifact produced by training — a set of learned parameters plus an architecture, that maps inputs to outputs. No. 5 Parameters & Weights The internal numeric values a model adjusts during training. A model's "size" (e.g. 7B, 70B) refers to its parameter count. ENGINEER’S NOTE think of parameters the way you'd think of a huge, tuned configuration file that training writes for you rather than one you write by hand. No. 6 Training vs. Inference Training is the (costly, offline) process of fitting parameters to data. Inference is the (cheap, online) act of running the finished model to get a prediction — analogous to build time versus runtime. No. 7 Dataset & Features The dataset is the collection of examples used for training or evaluation; features are the individual measurable inputs (columns, signals) describing each example. No. 8 Algorithm vs. Model The algorithm is the learning procedure itself (e.g. gradient descent); the model is what that procedure produces after being run over data.

II CHAPTER II Schools of Learning Every model is trained under one of these disciplines, or some blend thereof. Knowing which is in use tells you what data was needed and what the model can be trusted to do. No. 9 Supervised Learning Training on labeled examples — inputs paired with known correct outputs — so the model learns to reproduce that mapping on new data. No. 10 Unsupervised Learning Training on unlabeled data to discover structure on its own — clusters, groupings, or compressed representations — with no "correct answer" supplied. No. 11 Self-Supervised Learning A hybrid where labels are generated automatically from the data itself — for instance, predicting the next word in a sentence. This is how most large language models are pre-trained. No. 12 Reinforcement Learning (RL) An agent learns by taking actions in an environment and receiving rewards or penalties, gradually favoring the actions that yield greater long-term reward. No. 13 Transfer Learning Taking a model already trained on one large task and adapting it to a new, related task — reusing learned knowledge instead of starting from a blank slate. No. 14 Fine-Tuning Continuing to train an existing pre-trained model on a smaller, specific dataset so it specializes to a narrower task, domain, or tone.

III CHAPTER III The Neural Architectures The mechanical shapes into which parameters are arranged — each suited to a different sort of data. No. 15 Neural Network A model composed of layers of simple computational units ("neurons") connected by weighted links, loosely inspired by the brain's structure. No. 16 Activation Function A small non-linear function (e.g. ReLU, sigmoid) applied at each neuron, without which stacked layers would collapse into one plain linear equation. No. 17 CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) An architecture that slides small filters across an input — ideal for images — to detect local patterns like edges and textures. No. 18 RNN / LSTM Architectures that process sequences step by step, carrying a hidden memory forward. Largely superseded for language by the Transformer, but still seen in timeseries work. No. 19 Transformer The architecture (2017) behind nearly all modern LLMs. It processes an entire sequence at once using attention, rather than step by step, enabling far greater parallelism and scale. No. 20 Attention Mechanism A technique letting the model weigh how relevant every other token is to the one it is currently processing — the core innovation that lets Transformers capture longrange context. ENGINEER’S NOTE it behaves a little like a dynamic join: for each token, the model computes a relevance score against every other token before combining them. No. 21 Encoder–Decoder A two-part design: the encoder compresses an input into a representation, the decoder generates an output from it — used in translation and many sequence-tosequence tasks.

IV CHAPTER IV Training & Optimization The mechanics by which a model's parameters are nudged, iteration upon iteration, toward competence. No. 22 Loss Function A single number measuring how wrong the model's current predictions are. Training is, at heart, the continuous process of driving this number down. No. 23 Gradient Descent The optimization method that repeatedly nudges each parameter a small step in the direction that most reduces the loss. No. 24 Backpropagation The algorithm that efficiently computes how much each parameter contributed to the error, by propagating the loss backward through the network's layers. No. 25 Epoch, Batch & Learning Rate An epoch is one full pass over the training data; a batch is a small subset processed together per update step; the learning rate controls how large each parameter update is. No. 26 Overfitting & Underfitting Overfitting: the model memorizes training data but fails on new data. Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the pattern at all, and performs poorly everywhere. No. 27 Regularization Techniques (dropout, weight decay, etc.) deliberately added during training to discourage overfitting and improve generalization to unseen data. No. 28 RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) A fine-tuning stage where human preference judgments train a reward model, which then guides the LLM via reinforcement learning to produce more helpful, aligned responses.

CHAPTER V Large Language Models The vocabulary an engineer meets daily when integrating chat and completion models into real software. No. 29 LLM (Large Language Model) A Transformer-based model trained on vast text corpora to predict the next token, giving rise to broad abilities in writing, reasoning, and code. No. 30 Token & Tokenization Text is broken into tokens — pieces of words or characters — before a model can process it. Cost and context limits are almost always measured in tokens, not characters. No. 31 Context Window The maximum number of tokens (prompt plus response) a model can consider at once. Exceeding it means earlier content is truncated or dropped. ENGINEER’S NOTE treat it like a fixed-size buffer you must budget carefully — much like managing a limited request payload. No. 32 Embedding A dense vector of numbers representing the meaning of a word, sentence, or document, positioned such that semantically similar items sit close together in that vector space. No. 33 Prompt & Prompt Engineering The prompt is the input text given to a model; prompt engineering is the practice of crafting that input deliberately to reliably steer the model's output. No. 34 Zero-Shot / Few-Shot Zero-shot: asking a model to perform a task with no examples given. Few-shot: supplying a handful of examples within the prompt itself to demonstrate the desired pattern. No. 35 Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting a model to reason through intermediate steps aloud before giving a final answer, which tends to improve results on multi-step problems. No. 36 Temperature, Top-p & Top-k Sampling controls governing randomness at inference time: temperature scales overall unpredictability, while top-p and top-k restrict which candidate tokens are eligible to be chosen next. No. 37 Hallucination A confident but factually incorrect or fabricated output — a known failure mode arising because the model optimizes for plausible text, not verified truth. No. 38 System Prompt A privileged instruction set placed ahead of user input to establish a model's persona, rules, and constraints for the remainder of a conversation.

VI CHAPTER VI Retrieval, Agents & Tools How language models are wired into larger applications — the part of the field that looks most like the systems an engineer already builds. No. 39 RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) A pattern where relevant documents are fetched from an external store at query time and inserted into the prompt, grounding the model's answer in facts it wasn't trained on. ENGINEER’S NOTE architecturally, this is very like a cache-aside or read-through pattern, but the "cache" is a semantic index and the "reader" is the LLM. No. 40 Vector Database A database purpose-built to store embeddings and perform fast similarity search over them (e.g. Pinecone, Milvus, pgvector) — the retrieval half of RAG. No. 41 Semantic Search Search by meaning rather than exact keyword match, achieved by comparing the embedding of a query against embeddings of candidate documents. No. 42 Function Calling / Tool Use A capability letting a model emit a structured request to invoke an external function or API, with the result returned to it for further reasoning — the bridge between an LLM and your codebase. No. 43 Agent A system that uses an LLM in a loop — planning, calling tools, observing results, and iterating — to pursue a goal across multiple steps rather than answering in one shot. No. 44 MCP (Model Context Protocol) An open protocol standardizing how applications expose data sources and tools to LLMs, so a model can connect to many services through one consistent interface.

VII CHAPTER VII Generative Machinery The families of model responsible for producing wholly new content — text, image, sound. No. 45 Generative AI Models trained to produce new, original content — text, images, audio, or code — rather than merely classifying or scoring existing input. No. 46 GAN (Generative Adversarial Network) Two networks trained against each other — a generator producing fakes, a discriminator trying to catch them — until the generator's output is convincing. No. 47 Diffusion Model A generative approach that learns to reverse a gradual noising process, starting from pure noise and iteratively refining it into a coherent image or signal. No. 48 Latent Space A compressed, abstract coordinate space in which a model represents its data; moving through this space produces smooth, meaningful variations in generated output.

VIII CHAPTER VIII Engineering & Deployment The operational vocabulary of putting a trained model into production — the terrain most familiar to a backend engineer. No. 49 Model Serving / Inference Endpoint The runtime infrastructure that loads a trained model and exposes it behind an API for real-time or batch predictions — conceptually your familiar service layer, but GPU-bound. No. 50 Latency & Throughput Latency is time-to-first-token or time-to-full-response for one request; throughput is how many requests or tokens the system serves per second — the same trade-offs you already tune for any API. No. 51 Quantization Reducing the numeric precision of a model's weights (e.g. 32-bit to 4-bit) to shrink memory footprint and speed up inference, usually at a small cost in accuracy. No. 52 LoRA / PEFT Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning methods (Low-Rank Adaptation being the most common) that adapt a large model by training only a small set of additional weights, dramatically cutting cost. No. 53 Model Distillation Training a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher" model's outputs, yielding a lighter model that retains much of the teacher's capability. No. 54 GPU / TPU & VRAM Specialized processors (Graphics/Tensor Processing Units) built for the parallel matrix math of neural networks; VRAM is their onboard memory, which typically caps how large a model you can load. No. 55 Streaming Response Returning generated tokens to the client incrementally as they're produced, rather than waiting for the full output — much like chunked HTTP responses, and essential for perceived responsiveness.

IX CHAPTER IX Measures & Evaluation How the quality of a model, or of any single prediction, is scored and compared. No. 56 Accuracy, Precision & Recall Accuracy is overall correctness; precision is how many predicted positives were truly positive; recall is how many actual positives the model successfully found. No. 57 F1 Score The harmonic mean of precision and recall, used as a single balanced score when both false positives and false negatives matter. No. 58 Perplexity A measure of how "surprised" a language model is by real text; lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to what actually occurs. No. 59 Benchmark A standardized test set (e.g. MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K) used to compare different models' capabilities on a common, reproducible footing.

CHAPTER X Safety, Ethics & Governance The considerations any engineer shipping AI-driven features is now expected to reason about, not merely the model's authors. No. 60 Bias (Algorithmic) Systematic skew in a model's outputs, typically inherited from imbalances or prejudices present in its training data. No. 61 Alignment The broad effort to ensure a model's behavior matches human intentions and values, rather than optimizing its stated objective in unintended ways. No. 62 Guardrails Engineering controls — filters, validators, refusal policies — layered around a model in production to keep its behavior within acceptable bounds. No. 63 Prompt Injection An attack in which malicious instructions are smuggled into content a model processes (e.g. a webpage or document), attempting to hijack its behavior — the AIera analogue of injection attacks in traditional security. No. 64 Explainability (XAI) Techniques and tools aimed at making a model's internal reasoning or decision process interpretable to humans, rather than treating it as an opaque black box. Sixty-four terms, one chapter at a time: a foundation, not a ceiling. The field moves quickly; return to these pages, and add to them as you learn.
